query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid solidification processing (e.g., melt spinning) of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 followed by a controlled, short annealing step will produce an ultrafine, homogeneous microstructure with suppressed formation of brittle intergranular phases, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity (reducing cracking) while maintaining the high caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy that shows a coarse microstructure with brittle phases at grain boundaries leading to low mechanical robustness.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid solidification process (such as melt spinning) immediately after melting to refine the grain structure and then use a short, controlled annealing treatment to relieve residual stress without coarsening the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Under the same operational field/pressure conditions and temperature ranges used for caloric testing (room temperature up to moderate elevated temperatures), and under typical mechanical loading regimes where cracking is observed.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, ultrafine-grained microstructure with predominantly coherent grain boundaries and a minimized volume fraction of brittle precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Rapid solidification limits the diffusion necessary for the growth of brittle intergranular phases and encourages a homogeneous dispersion of phases. The refined microstructure increases crack blunting and impedes crack propagation while preserving the lattice transformations (or other phase-change mechanisms) that underlie the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in compressive strength (targeting improvements from ~150 MPa to 150–250 MPa or higher) and reduced tendency for cracking, with the magnitude of the caloric response retained within approximately 10% of that of the unprocessed alloy.
generation.baseline: The baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but suffers from poor structural integrity manifested as cracking under load.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under conditions typical for caloric operation (moderate temperature, field, and mechanical load environments). Extreme processing or operational conditions that might induce unforeseen phase instability or significant diffusion could negate the improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise balance between microstructural refinement and preservation of the caloric mechanism is not fully quantified; thus, the optimal cooling rate and annealing parameters need experimental fine tuning. It is also uncertain whether any subtle change in the microstructure might slightly affect the magnitude of the caloric effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples: one using conventional casting and the other using rapid solidification (e.g., melt spinning) followed by a controlled annealing step. Characterize both sets with respect to microstructure (using SEM/TEM), mechanical properties (compressive strength and crack propagation via standardized mechanical tests), and caloric response (using differential scanning calorimetry or direct caloric effect measurements under applied magnetic/pressure fields).
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase analysis (SEM/TEM, XRD)
Mechanical integrity: compressive strength and strain-to-failure tests
Caloric response magnitude (enthalpy change per field change)
Crack initiation and propagation analysis under mechanical loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid solidification processed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical properties (e.g., less than a 10% increase in compressive strength or similar crack resistance) or if the caloric response decreases by more than approximately 10% compared to the conventional samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.
